prompt.context: Our client is a large pharmaceutical company with a strong business in 'Rare Disease' (rare diseases are conditions that affect fewer than 200,000 people in the US). Historically, pharmaceutical companies have not invested significantly in Rare Disease because it has not been cost effective to conduct research for such small populations. Due to the fall off in the number of pharmaceutical blockbusters and improved regulation to make R&D cheaper for Rare Disease, pharmaceutical companies have begun to invest more in Rare Disease R&D over the last few years. Our client has hired BCG because it would like to grow its Rare Disease business.
prompt.question: How can the client double its Rare Disease business in 5 years?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the client's existing Rare Disease business and how fast is it growing?
clarifying_info.a: The client is an industry leader with a track record of success. Its existing business is $2.5B, expected to grow at 5% per year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size and profitability of the overall Rare Disease market?
clarifying_info.a: The Rare Disease market is $30B and is as profitable as Big Pharma. While research is relatively expensive, the government provides tax credits for drugs designated to treat rare diseases. Additionally, prices tend to be higher to make up for the upfront research investment. It is also growing faster than Big Pharma.
There are many small bio-techs that are attractive targets, and there are also other big pharmaceutical companies that have rare disease divisions and assets.

exhibits.title: Assets in Research and Development
exhibits.shows: A table showing the client's R&D pipeline by phase, including number of assets, time to market (years), attrition rate (% expected to be approved and reach the market), and peak revenue per asset. A second table shows revenue ramp by year on market as a percentage of peak revenue.

framework: Quantify the gap: project organic growth from existing business and pipeline assets by 2016/year 5, then calculate the shortfall vs. the $5B doubling target
Organic growth lever 1 — existing portfolio: apply the 5% annual growth rate to the $2.5B baseline over 5 years

Organic growth lever 2 — pipeline: use the Exhibit 1 data to estimate revenue contribution from Phase I, II, and III assets that will reach market within 5 years (Research assets take 6 years and will not contribute)
Inorganic growth lever — acquisitions: determine how much additional revenue is needed and how many 'peak revenue' assets must be acquired to close the gap
Synthesize: propose a portfolio mix (organic + acquisitions) that achieves the $5B target, and outline risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1 data, how large will the client's Rare Disease business be in 2016 (year 5)? What is the shortfall to its goal of doubling the business?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will systematically work through three buckets: (1) existing business growth, (2) pipeline contribution by phase, and (3) sum to find the gap vs. $5B target. They should note that Research assets (6-year time to market) will NOT contribute within 5 years.

math.setup: Existing business: $2.5B growing at 5%/year for 5 years (linear approximation). Pipeline: for each phase, apply attrition to get approved assets, then apply the revenue ramp percentage corresponding to how many years that asset will have been on market by year 5. Target = $2.5B * 2 = $5B.
steps: Existing business growth: $2.5B * 5% * 5 = $625M additional; baseline in year 5 = $2.5B + $625M = $3.125B
Research assets: time to market = 6 years > 5 years, so $0M contribution
Phase I: 5 assets * 20% attrition = 1 approved asset; reaches market in year 4 of the 5-year window, so it will be in its 1st year on market at year 5; revenue = 1 * $500M * 20% = $100M
Phase II: 3 assets * 40% attrition = 1.2 approved assets; reaches market in year 3 of the 5-year window, so it will be in its 2nd year on market at year 5; revenue = 1.2 * $500M * 40% = $240M
Phase III: 1 asset * 60% attrition = 0.6 approved assets; reaches market in year 2 of the 5-year window, so it will be in its 3rd year on market at year 5; revenue = 0.6 * $500M * 60% = $180M
Total internal growth by year 5: $3.125B + $520M = approximately $3.645B (the casebook rounds pipeline total to $520M and existing growth to $625M, giving $3.125B + $0.520B = $3.645B)
math.answer: The client's business will reach approximately $3.645B organically by year 5, leaving a shortfall of approximately $1.4B to reach the $5B doubling target.

questions.prompt: What does the client need to do to double the Rare Disease revenues by 2016? Specifically, who to acquire and how many assets will be needed?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify acquisitions as the lever to close the ~$1.4B gap. They should calculate the number of peak-revenue assets needed: $1.4B gap / $500M peak revenue per asset ≈ 3 assets. They should also note that more assets would be needed if targets are in R&D rather than already at peak revenue. Strong candidates will discuss target types (small bio-techs vs. divisions of large pharma) and mention integration and execution risks.

math.setup: Gap to close = ~$1.4B. Each acquired 'peak revenue' asset generates $500M.
steps: Number of peak revenue assets needed: $1.4B / $500M = 2.8, rounded up to approximately 3 assets
If assets are in earlier R&D stages, more acquisitions would be needed to account for attrition and ramp-up time
math.answer: The client needs to acquire approximately 3 peak-revenue assets to close the ~$1.4B gap.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the different ways the client could grow its Rare Disease business?

categories.name: Organic — existing portfolio
ideas: Expand approved indications for existing drugs
Improve commercial execution and market penetration

categories.name: Organic — pipeline acceleration
ideas: Increase R&D investment to advance pipeline assets faster
Partner with academic institutions or CROs to reduce time to market
Prioritize higher-attrition-rate pipeline assets for faster development

categories.name: Inorganic — acquisitions
ideas: Acquire small bio-tech companies with promising Rare Disease assets
Acquire Rare Disease divisions from large pharmaceutical companies
Acquire assets at peak revenue to generate immediate revenue
Acquire earlier-stage assets at lower cost with higher future upside

categories.name: Partnerships and licensing
ideas: Co-development agreements to share R&D costs
Licensing deals for approved drugs in new markets
Joint ventures with other pharma companies in the Rare Disease space

recommendation: Internal organic growth alone will not be sufficient to achieve the goal of doubling the Rare Disease business to $5B in 5 years; the existing portfolio and pipeline will generate approximately $3.645B, leaving a ~$1.4B shortfall

The client should pursue approximately 3 acquisitions of peak-revenue Rare Disease assets to close the gap, resulting in a 2016 portfolio of approximately $5B: ~$3.1B from the current baseline (60%), ~$520M from the pipeline (10%), and ~$1.4B from acquisitions (30%)
risks: Acquisition targets may not be available at acceptable valuations given increased competition for Rare Disease assets
Acquired assets may face regulatory or clinical setbacks
Integration of acquired bio-techs or divisions may be complex
Pipeline assets may face higher-than-expected attrition
Organic growth rate of 5% may not be sustained if existing drugs face competition or patent expiry
next_steps: Conduct a detailed screen of potential acquisition targets (small bio-techs and pharma Rare Disease divisions) and assess strategic fit, valuation, and integration complexity
Assess ability to accelerate existing pipeline assets to reduce reliance on acquisitions
Develop a detailed integration playbook for acquired assets
Monitor Rare Disease market dynamics and competitive landscape
